steps.description: This is a pure machine learning / mathematical experiment to probe "solution space rigidity" using small feedforward networks as probes. I will design an experiment where a function f(x) is defined with known analytical constraints (e.g., boundary conditions, symmetry constraints, or functional equations), and I will vary the number of constraints w and the network hidden width N to find the minimal N_c(w) that achieves zero violation (max absolute error ≤ 1e-3) on held-out constraint points. The rigidity claim is tested by observing whether N_c(w) remains small and bounded as w increases. I will implement a multi-layer perceptron in PyTorch, train it on constraint satisfaction (not data fitting), and sweep widths from 4 to 64 for w = 4, 8, 12, 16. I will report N_c(w) values and whether they saturate (rigid) or grow unbounded (fat).

To rigorously test the Gradient Flow Rigidity Hypothesis, we will design a numerical experiment to determine the minimal network width $N_c(w)$ required to satisfy $w$ analytical constraints with zero violation ($\max |error| \le 1e-3$) on held-out points. We will define a family of smooth analytical functions, sample $w$ constraints, train small feedforward networks with varying hidden widths, and compute the out-of-sample maximum absolute error to identify the transition from "fat" (underfitting) to "rigid" (exact satisfaction) behavior.

We will design a numerical experiment to test the hypothesis that small feedforward networks exhibit "rigid" solution space (i.e., a finite critical width $N_c$ where zero-violation is achieved on held-out constraints) as a function of constraint count $w$. Steps: (1) Define a simple analytical constraint set (e.g., polynomial interpolation or trigonometric fitting) with $w$ points; (2) Train small feedforward networks (1-2 hidden layers, width $N$ from 4 to 64) on $w$ training points; (3) Evaluate max absolute error on a held-out test set of $w$ points; (4) Record $N_c(w)$ as the minimal width where max error $\le 1e-3$; (5) Repeat for increasing $w$ to check if $N_c$ remains small and bounded. If $N_c$ stays low and finite across $w$, we conclude rigidity; if no width achieves zero violation, we conclude "fat". This directly tests the hypothesis using pure ML/math tools without physical mapping.

To test the "Stochastic Initialization Boundedness Hypothesis" regarding solution space rigidity, I will perform a numerical scan of small feedforward networks. Specifically, I will define a deterministic function with analytic constraints (e.g., a polynomial or trigonometric combination) and sample $w$ points from it. I will then train networks of varying hidden widths $N$ on these $w$ points using stochastic initialization, evaluating whether a "zero-violation" state (max absolute error $\le 10^{-3}$ on held-out constraints) is achieved. The goal is to determine if there exists a finite capacity $N_c(w)$ that remains bounded as $w$ increases (rigid) or if capacity must grow indefinitely (fat). This aligns with the requirement to treat this as a pure ML/math problem without physical reduction.
